newsitem.title: UK: Volatile nickel reclaims some gains, copper firms.
newsitem.headline: Volatile nickel reclaims some gains, copper firms.

text.p: Nickel grabbed back some of its early rally gains during the morning kerb on the London Metal Exchange on Tuesday after initially shedding some $300 in a hectic day's trading.
Flagship copper also shot higher towards $2,500 resistance after a late-breaking shortcovering rally lifted it from the $2,470-$2,475 support level.
But aluminium showed the scars from persistent long liquidation and the other metals displayed little life of their own.

In the lively nickel market, Far Eastern buying had whisked three months nickel to a peak of $7,330 per tonne in the early pre-market following news of a strike at Inco's Sudbury operation, traders said.

But the knee-jerk spike higher was rapidly sold off to a low of $7,020 by the morning rings and trading slowed to a crawl until a spate of shortcovering emerged on the kerb. It ended at $7,180 compared to Monday's afternoon kerb close of $7,025.

One trader that nickel was in a $7,000-$7,250 range for now but a break lower was possible and would target $6,700. News that Russia's Norilsk aimed to increase output by 20 percent this year also helped diminish the bullishness of the Inco news.
A sickly mood pervaded the other base metals ahead of the kerb, with flagship copper flirting with support in the $2,470-$2,480 area. But it bounced sharply at the end to finish $6 firmer at $2,491.
"It's actually quite remarkable that copper started the kerb looking terrible at $2,475 and finished at $2,491," a trader said.
The market was anxious ahead of Wednesday's options declaration, and copper's tumble below the 10-day moving average on Monday had given the market the jitters, another said.

Aluminium ploughed lower, only slightly boosted by copper's firmness, on what traders attributed in part to long liquidation by a large investment house. Its break through the $1,600 level on Monday left it vulnerable to further losses, traders said.
A slow-down in physical demand ahead of the traditionally quiet third quarter was bruising sentiment, as was the spread at a $20 contango, compared to $10 in recent weeks.
While aluminium was finding some support at $1,580, traders said it would be sold down again if it attempted a move to $1,600.
The other metals were generally quiet.
Zinc continues to suffer from talk that more Chinese metal is due for delivery in Singapore warehouses and was down $4 at $1,326. A test of $1,310-$1,315 support was possible, traders said.
Lead was off $2 at $624, and tin was up $10 at $5,650. Alloy was quiet and indicated some $7 easier at $1,473/78.
